1. Core Clinical Tension: A 37-year-old Ethiopian man presented with a 3-year history of intermittent abdominal pain and bilious vomiting, acutely worsening over 3 months with marked weight loss, severe anemia, and cross-sectional imaging demonstrating multifocal small bowel strictures and necrotic mesenteric lymphadenopathy. The clinical challenge is distinguishing primary intestinal tuberculosis from Crohn's disease and small bowel adenocarcinoma in a patient with a completely normal chest radiograph.
2. Admission Breakpoint: The admission breakpoint occurs following admission triage, baseline laboratory evaluation (demonstrating anemia with normal metabolic and liver panels), normal chest radiography, abdominal ultrasound, and contrast-enhanced abdominal CT, prior to trial of immunosuppressive therapy (hydrocortisone) and exploratory laparotomy with surgical resection.
3. Differential Distinctions: Small bowel adenocarcinoma was suspected based on ultrasound showing an asymmetric mass-like lesion but was excluded by multifocal concentric strictures and absent neoplastic cells on surgical pathology. Crohn's disease presents with identical transmural strictures, skip lesions, and chronicity, but necrotic hypoattenuating lymph nodes on CT and caseating granulomas with Langhans giant cells on histopathology definitively established intestinal tuberculosis.
case_prompt:
A 37-year-old man in Sidama, Ethiopia, presented to a specialized internal medicine clinic with a 3-month worsening of crampy, intermittent abdominal pain. He reported a 3-year history of recurrent abdominal discomfort, episodic abdominal distension, and intermittent vomiting of ingested meals with occasional bilious content. Over the past 3 months, his symptoms had intensified, accompanied by progressive constipation without complete obstipation (retaining ability to pass flatus and stool), profound easy fatigability, anorexia, and marked unquantified weight loss. He reported no diarrhea, hematochezia, cough, fever, or prior medical conditions.

On physical examination, he appeared chronically ill and acutely uncomfortable. The pulse rate was 104 beats per minute, respiratory rate was 20 breaths per minute, blood pressure was 100/70 mmHg, and he was afebrile to touch. Examination of the conjunctivae revealed mild pallor. The abdomen was soft, moved symmetrically with respiration, and demonstrated no visible peristalsis, localized tenderness, guarding, or palpable masses. Digital rectal examination was unremarkable.

Laboratory studies demonstrated a hemoglobin level of 8.4 g/dL and hematocrit of 27.9%. The white-cell count was 6,500 per cubic millimeter (73% granulocytes and 15% lymphocytes) and platelet count was 295,000 per cubic millimeter. Fasting blood glucose, blood urea nitrogen, serum creatinine, electrolytes, and liver biochemistries (AST, ALT, alkaline phosphatase) were all within normal limits. A plain chest radiograph was normal.

An abdominal ultrasound revealed a 4.5 x 2.2 cm asymmetric short-segment small bowel wall thickening in the left upper quadrant with a maximum wall thickness of 1.2 cm, accompanied by enlarged adjacent mesenteric lymph nodes (up to 1.1 cm) and proximal small bowel dilatation up to 5 cm with collapsed distal loops, indicative of partial small bowel obstruction. Subsequent abdominal CT showed multifocal short- and long-segment symmetric small bowel wall thickening predominantly in the left lower quadrant, producing luminal narrowing, shouldering, and upstream loop dilatation. Multifocal luminal constrictions were visible, along with mesenteric fat stranding and small mesenteric lymph nodes exhibiting central hypoattenuation consistent with internal necrosis.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Raised due to ultrasound findings of asymmetric focal bowel wall thickening, luminal stenosis, proximal dilation, and regional mesenteric lymphadenopathy; ruled out by cross-sectional CT demonstrating multifocal concentric skip-like strictures and surgical pathology confirming granulomatous inflammation rather than adenocarcinoma.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: The conclusion was, short segment small bowel wall thickening with luminal stenosis and features of partial SBO (Small bowel obstruction) and mesenteric lymphadenopathies, and small bowel carcinoma was considered as differential diagnosis, and Abdominal CT (Computed tomography) was recommended.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Strongly considered given the 3-year indolent history, crampy postprandial pain, weight loss, multifocal small bowel strictures, and shouldering; excluded by the presence of centrally necrotic lymphadenopathy and histological confirmation of caseating necrosis, with failure of initial response to corticosteroids.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: The patient was admitted with the consideration of Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) and was given IV Ceftriaxone and Hydrocortisone and kept on maintenance fluid for 36hrs.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: CT identification of multifocal small bowel constrictions alongside centrally hypoattenuating (necrotic) mesenteric lymph nodes, followed by surgical resection revealing concentric strictures and histopathology confirming epithelioid cell aggregates, Langhans giant cells, and central caseous necrosis, established intestinal tuberculosis.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: Small mesenteric lymph nodes were noted in the left lower quadrant small bowel mesentery with adjacent mesenteric fat stranding and internal hypoattenuation in keeping with central necrosis (see Figure 1)... The microscopic description of the Pathology report stated: Sections from the intestinal lesions and mesenteric lymph nodes revealed nodular aggregates of epitheloid cells surrounded by mixed inflammatory cells and scattered Langhans type giant cells with areas of central caseous necrosis. That was histomorphologically consistent with Tuberculosis

editor_comments: Presentation strictly halts at the admission breakpoint after CT imaging. Operative findings, steroids/antibiotics trial, and histopathological analysis are strictly confined to the diagnostic reasoning.
